questions.prompt: An LTI system has input \(x(t)\), impulse response \(h(t)\) and output \(y(t)=h(t)\ast x(t)\). In the frequency domain, what does this convolution become?
options: An addition: \(Y(s)=H(s)+X(s)\)
A convolution again: \(Y=H\ast X\)
A multiplication: \(Y(s)=H(s)\cdot X(s)\)
A division: \(Y(s)=X(s)/H(s)\)
questions.explanation: Convolution in time becomes multiplication in the (Laplace/Fourier) frequency domain: \(Y=H\cdot X\) (reader Eq. 1.90). That is why filters are easiest to understand in the frequency domain: each frequency component of the input is just multiplied by H at that frequency.

questions.prompt: How is the frequency response \(H(j\omega)\) of an LTI circuit related to its impulse response \(h(t)\)?
options: \(H(j\omega)\) is the derivative of \(h(t)\) with respect to \(\omega\)
\(H(j\omega)\) is the Fourier (Laplace) transform of \(h(t)\), i.e., \(H(s)\) evaluated on the imaginary axis \(s=j\omega\)
\(H(j\omega)=h(t)\) evaluated at \(t=\omega\)
They are unrelated: one is for sinusoids and the other for impulses
questions.explanation:
\(H(s)=\int h(t)e^{-st}\ dt\) (the Laplace transform), and \(H(j\omega)\) is that function evaluated at \(s=j\omega\) (reader Eq. 1.86 and 1.94). The impulse response and the transfer function are two descriptions of the same system.
The other options are not valid relationships.

questions.prompt: A filter has \(|H|=0.5\) at 1 kHz and \(|H|=0.1\) at 3 kHz. The input is the sum of a 2 V (amplitude) tone at 1 kHz and a 2 V tone at 3 kHz. What is the amplitude of the 3 kHz tone at the output?
questions.explanation:
Each input frequency is multiplied by the filter's gain at that frequency. 3 kHz tone: \(2\ \mathrm{V}\times 0.1=0.2\ \mathrm{V}\). The 1 kHz tone becomes \(2\times 0.5=1\ \mathrm{V}\). The tones do not interact because the system is linear.
Common mistake: using the 1 kHz gain (0.5) for both tones.

questions.prompt: An LTI system has impulse response \(h(t)=200\cdot e^{-t/2\ \mathrm{ms}}\cdot u(t)\ \mathrm{s}^{-1}\). Using \(H(0)=\int h(t)dt\), what is its DC gain?
questions.explanation:
At \(\omega=0\ (s=0)\) the transform integral reduces to \(H(0)=\int_{0}^{\infty}h(t)\ dt\): the area under the impulse response.
\(\int_{0}^{\infty}200e^{-t/2\ \mathrm{ms}}\ dt=200\times 2\ \mathrm{ms}=0.4\). So the DC gain is 0.4.
Common mistake: using \(h(0)=200\) as the gain.

questions.prompt: A system has impulse response \(h(t)=(1/\tau)e^{-t/\tau}u(t)\) with \(\tau=0.5\ \mathrm{ms}\). Using \(H(j\omega)=\int_{0}^{\infty}h(t)e^{-j\omega t}dt=(1/\tau)/(1/\tau+j\omega)\), what is |H| at \(f=500\ \mathrm{Hz}\)?
questions.explanation:
\(\omega=2\pi\cdot 500=3141.6\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\) and \(1/\tau=2000\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\).
\(|H|=2000/\sqrt{2000^{2}+3141.6^{2}}=2000/3724.1=0.537\).
Equivalently \(H(j\omega)=1/(1+j\omega\tau)\) with \(\omega\tau=1.571\), so \(|H|=1/\sqrt{1+2.467}=0.537\). Common mistake: using f instead of \(\omega\ (\omega\tau=0.25\) gives 0.970).
questions.figure_alt: Single-pole magnitude response with its corner near 318 hertz and a marked point at 500 hertz.

questions.prompt: A single-pole filter has \(H(jf)=1/(1+jf/1\ \mathrm{kHz})\). The input is the sum of a 1 kHz tone of amplitude 2 V and a 10 kHz tone of amplitude 1 V. What are the output tone amplitudes?
options: 1 kHz: 1 V, 10 kHz: 0.091 V
1 kHz: 1.414 V, 10 kHz: 1 V
questions.explanation:
\(|H(1\ \mathrm{kHz})|=1/\sqrt{1+1^{2}}=0.7071\) ⇒ \(2\times 0.7071=1.414\ \mathrm{V}\).
\(|H(10\ \mathrm{kHz})|=1/\sqrt{1+10^{2}}=1/\sqrt{101}=0.0995\) ⇒ \(1\times 0.0995=0.0995\ \mathrm{V}\).
• '1 V and 0.091 V' uses \(1/(1+f/f_{c})\) instead of \(1/\sqrt{1+(f/f_{c})^{2}}\): gains of 0.5 and 0.091.
• '2 V' wrongly assumes the passband tone at the corner is unattenuated; at \(f_{c}\) the gain is 0.707.
• '1 V' for the 10 kHz tone ignores the filter entirely.
questions.figure_alt: Asymptotic and exact magnitude of a single-pole filter with a 1 kilohertz corner.

questions.prompt: A circuit is an ALL-PASS network: \(|H(j\omega)|=1\) at every frequency, but its phase is not a linear function of \(\omega\). A signal made of several sinusoids passes through it. What can happen to the waveform?
options: Nothing: equal magnitude at all frequencies guarantees an identical waveform
Only the overall amplitude can change, by a common factor
New frequencies appear, since the phase is non-linear
The shape can change, because different frequencies are delayed by different amounts of time, even though each tone keeps its amplitude
questions.explanation:
A waveform's shape depends on the relative phases of its frequency components as well as their amplitudes. If \(\angle H\) is not proportional to \(\omega\), the tones are shifted by different times and add up differently. The all-pass network keeps each tone's amplitude but can still distort the waveform ('phase distortion'). Only a linear phase (a pure delay) preserves the shape.
• Equal magnitudes alone do not guarantee an undistorted waveform.
• Amplitudes of the individual tones are unchanged, so it is not a uniform amplitude scaling.
• An LTI system never creates new frequencies.

questions.prompt: A low-pass filter has \(H(jf)=1/(1+jf/1\ \mathrm{kHz})\). The input is \(v_{\mathrm{in}}=4+3\cos(2\pi\cdot 1\ \mathrm{kHz}\cdot t)+2\cos(2\pi\cdot 10\ \mathrm{kHz}\cdot t)\) volts. What is the RMS value of the steady-state output? (Tones at different frequencies contribute to mean-square power additively; a DC term contributes its value squared.)
questions.explanation:
Output components: DC: \(4\ \mathrm{V}\times H(0)=4\ \mathrm{V}\). 1 kHz: \(3\times 0.7071=2.121\ \mathrm{V}\) peak. 10 kHz: \(2/\sqrt{101}=0.199\ \mathrm{V}\) peak.
Mean square \(=4^{2}+(2.121^{2})/2+(0.199^{2})/2=16+2.25+0.0198=18.27\).
\(RMS=\sqrt{18.27}=4.274\ \mathrm{V}\).
Common mistakes: adding peak amplitudes (6.3 V), or dividing the DC term by \(\sqrt{2}\ (DC\) is already its own RMS value).

questions.prompt: Which statement about \(H(s)\) and \(H(j\omega)\) of a stable LTI circuit is correct?
options: \(H(j\omega)\) describes the transient response and \(H(s)\) describes the steady state
\(H(j\omega)\) and \(H(s)\) are different functions with no mathematical relationship

\(H(j\omega)\) is \(H(s)\) evaluated on the imaginary axis; it gives the steady-state response to sinusoids, while \(H(s)\) also describes inputs of the form \(e^{st}\) with a decaying or growing real part
\(H(j\omega)\) is only defined for \(\omega>0\), and the response at \(-\omega\) is unrelated to it
questions.explanation:
Setting \(s=j\omega\) in \(H(s)\) gives the frequency response: the eigenvalue of the system for sinusoidal (periodic) complex exponentials, hence the steady-state sinusoidal response. The general \(H(s)\) (any \(s=\sigma+j\omega\)) gives the response to est, which includes transient behavior (reader Sec. 1.6.2 and 1.10.1).
• The roles are reversed in the first wrong option.
• They are the same function on different parts of the complex plane.
• For real circuits \(H(-j\omega)=H(j\omega)*\), so negative frequencies carry no new information; they are related.

questions.prompt: Preview of noise. A later skill says that white noise with density \(e_{n}\ (V/\sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}})\) passing through a filter of gain |H| over a bandwidth B has RMS value \(e_{n}\cdot|H|\cdot\sqrt{B}\). An amplifier output has flat noise density \(20\ \mathrm{nV}/\sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}}\). A filter with \(|H|=0.5\) from 0 to 1 kHz (and essentially 0 above) follows it. What is the RMS noise at the filter output, in nV?
questions.explanation:
\(v_{n}=e_{n}\cdot|H|\cdot\sqrt{B}=20\ \mathrm{nV}/\sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}}\times 0.5\times\sqrt{1000}\ \mathrm{Hz}=20\times 0.5\times 31.62=316.2\ \mathrm{nV}\ (RMS)\).
This is the 'filtering reduces noise' idea from Fig. 1.24: only the noise inside the passband gets through. Common mistake: forgetting the square root of the bandwidth (giving 10 µV).

questions.prompt: Preview of op-amp frequency response. A closed-loop op-amp amplifier with a low-frequency gain of 10 has the single-pole response \(H(jf)=10/(1+jf/100\ \mathrm{kHz})\). For a 0.1 V amplitude tone at 1 MHz, what is the output amplitude?
questions.explanation:
At \(f=1\ \mathrm{MHz}\), \(f/f_{c}=10\): \(|H|=10/\sqrt{1+100}=10/10.05=0.995\).
Output amplitude \(=0.1\ \mathrm{V}\times 0.995=0.0995\ \mathrm{V}\) (the gain has fallen from 10 to about 1).
Common mistake: using the low-frequency gain of 10 (1 V). This is exactly the frequency-domain limit on how well an amplifier tracks fast signals.

questions.prompt: Preview of dynamic errors in feedback. An ideal closed-loop amplifier would have \(H=1\), but a real one has \(H(j\omega)=1/(1+j\omega/\omega_{c})\). At a frequency \(\omega=0.2\omega_{c}\), by what percentage is the MAGNITUDE of the gain below 1? (error \(=(1-|H|)\times 100\%\))
questions.explanation:
\(|H|=1/\sqrt{1+0.2^{2}}=1/\sqrt{1.04}=0.98058\).
Magnitude error \(=(1-0.98058)\times 100\%=1.942\%\).
Note the phase error \((-\tan^{-1}\ 0.2=-11.3^{\circ})\) is also significant. Common mistake: answering 20% (confusing the ratio \(\omega/\omega_{c}\) with the error). For small \(\omega/\omega_{c}\) the magnitude error is only about \(\tfrac{1}{2}(\omega/\omega_{c})^{2}=2\%\), because the magnitude depends on the SQUARE of the ratio.
questions.figure_alt: Single-pole closed-loop magnitude with a marked point at 0.2 omega_c, slightly below 0 dB.
